comment: Items are CONTENT, like materials.json and glyphs.json â€” not look-and-feel knobs like tuning.json. This file holds an item's BEHAVIOUR: its id, the kind the engine switches on, and its damage numbers. THE ART IS NOT HERE, and it is not part of any creature either: each item owns <id>.vox plus an <id>.json sidecar carrying its grip and its cutting edge. A held item BORROWS a rig slot, so while worn it is a real rig part â€” severable with the arm, droppable as debris, carvable per voxel â€” but its geometry has its own origin, so a weapon can never inflate the box of the body holding it. That was a real bug: as a rig prop the sword reached 30 micro outside mina's prefab box and drew her body offset from her own arm. Hot-reloads on R alongside materials and glyphs.
kinds: melee = swung, and cuts along the `edge` segment its own sidecar declares (see scripts/gen_sword_item.py). The blade geometry is what decides the wound; `carveBonus` only widens it. A HIT IS THREE PARTS (src/game/impact.h): `damage` is the CUT part (the key is not renamed -- it is still the honest name for the half of a blow that opens a wound), `blunt` is trauma that charges hp and bruises without ever dismembering, and `bite` is a tear (authored on creatures, not on items). `bluntCarve` and `armorBreak` are 0..1 fractions of a tuning radius -- how much of gore.bluntCarveRadius a blow dents out of flesh, and how much of gear.bluntDentRadius it breaks out of a worn shell. That is why a mace beats plate and a sword does not. container = a vessel (src/game/container.h): `container.holds` names the material CLASSES it takes up (liquid, powder), `capacity` is in cells, the rates are cells per tick, `throwSpeedMps`/`throwMinSpeedMps`/`throwChargeSec` are the Q throw (speed at full charge, on a tap, and how long the wind-up takes; 0 = not thrown), `breakSpeedMps` the closing speed that shatters it (0 = never), `fillSlices` is how many x-slices of the model, from its base up, are see-through -- a held vessel shows its contents there, in their own colour and up to the level their volume reaches (0 = the contents are hidden, as in the leather pouch), and `applyCells` is how many cells a second of pouring on your own body (the character screen's portrait brush) spends at the default brush size -- it scales with the brush's area. The flask and the pouch are the same kind; what differs is data. shield = held in a hand like a weapon, but that hand's button RAISES it; what it stops is its own voxels in their live pose (see the SHIELDS row below for the `shield` block).

items.//heft: Pinned, not derived: the old 40/m slab measured 5.31 world voxels (= gore.woundHeftRef), the 80/m blade with a real section measures far less while weighing the same.
items.desc: A straight double-edged arming sword. Held point-up; it cuts with the length of its blade, so where you land it is where the wound opens.
A two-handed cleaver, wide at the tip and heavy with it. It is not quicker than a sword and it is not subtler; it simply arrives with more behind the edge, and takes a limb in a third of the blows.

items.//heft: Pinned to what the 40/m art derived (212 micro / 4^3 / 5.3).
items.desc: Two feet of straight double-edged blade on a one-hand grip. It gives up the arming sword's last third of reach and about a third of its weight with it, and hands back a weapon you can still swing inside somebody's guard.

items.//heft: Pinned to what the 40/m art derived (76 micro / 4^3 / 5.3).
items.desc: A hand's length of point, and barely a fifth of the sword behind it. It will not take an arm off in one pass and it was never going to; what it does is open the same wound over and over while standing closer than a sword can answer.

A flanged head on a short wrapped haft. It has almost no edge and does not want one: what it does is arrive, and a man in plate is still a man with a plate-shaped dent in him. Against an unarmoured body it bruises and caves rather than opening, so it will hammer somebody to death without ever taking an arm off.
A deep cloth cowl. It keeps the rain off and catches fire readily; what it will not do is stop a blade.
A heavy black robe, sleeves to the wrist and a skirt to the knee. Cloth over skin: fire reaches the cloth first.
A gold-shot band worn at the waist, over the robe.
Grey wool trousers, cut straight and ending where a boot begins. Nothing about them will turn an edge; they are what stands between your legs and the weather.
Cut leather, slow to catch. Better against a spill than against a fire.
A close iron helm with one slit across the eyes. Iron over the skull: fire finds nothing on it to catch, and acid pits it a grain at a time instead of eating it.

An iron breastplate with a gorget at the throat, a yoke across both shoulders, plate down each arm to the wrist and a short fauld over the hips. It does not burn. Acid takes it slowly, and a blade takes it not at all until it has beaten it in.
Iron cuisses and greaves, thigh to ankle. Heavy, fireproof, and slow to dissolve.
Iron shoes with an ankle cuff. What a spill of acid meets first, and what it gets through last.

Articulated iron over the back of each hand, with a cuff to the wrist. They will not stop much on their own; what they change is what your fists are for. A bare hand bruises. These cave a face in, a little at a time, and beat another man's plate while they do it.
A pull-over linen tunic, sleeves to the elbow and a body to mid-thigh, laced at the throat. What most people are wearing most of the time. It takes a dye evenly and it stops nothing.
A long working smock, full sleeves with cuffs and cloth enough in the skirt to move in. Mended once at the hem already; it will be mended again.
A sleeveless leather jerkin laced up the front, cut off at the waist. Bare shoulders, a bound armhole, and rather more between a blade and your ribs than linen manages.
Straight linen trousers, seamed down the outside of each leg and hemmed where a shoe begins.
Knee breeches, tied below the knee and leaving the calf to the weather. Worn with wraps, or with boots, or with nothing.
Close linen hose, gartered at the thigh and darned at one knee. Nothing about them is in the way, which is the only thing they have to recommend them.
Low leather shoes with a stitched sole and a lace across the instep. Better than bare feet on a road and worse than boots anywhere else.
Wooden clogs on a block sole, an inch of hardwood between you and the mud. They do not soak, they do not rot, and they burn like the log they were.
Strips of linen wound round the foot and crossed at the ankle. The cheapest thing that is not going barefoot, and the first thing to catch.

A stoppered glass flask. Hold the right button over any liquid to fill it, the left to pour it where you are looking. With the character screen open, hold the left button on your portrait to pour it exactly where the cursor is -- over a wound, or a burn, or yourself. Hold Q to wind up a throw and let go to hurl it; it is glass, and whatever it hits hard enough -- or whatever hits it -- breaks it and lets everything inside out at once.
A drawstring leather pouch for anything that pours but is not wet: sand, ash, dust, seed. Right button to scoop, left to scatter it where you look.

items.//: KEYS (dungeons D3, docs/PLAN_dungeons.md 3.7): kind key = carried, never held or worn. A door whose props.lock names this key's keyId opens for whoever has it in the kit (bag or hotbar). `unlocks` names the keyId; absent = the item's own id. Art: scripts/gen_key_items.py.
items.desc: A plain iron key. Somewhere there is a door that has been waiting for it.
A key carved from a long bone. The crypts of the old temple were locked with these.
A heavy black key, its bit worn smooth by a century of turning.

items.//: THE BOW AND ARROWS (docs/PLAN_projectiles.md C, game/arrows.h). A bow is kind melee so it rides a hand slot like any weapon, but weaponClass `bow` takes it out of the stroke system: with it in hand the hand's button DRAWS (held) and SHOOTS (released). `bow.drawSpeedMps` is the arrow's speed at full draw, `windupMs` how long raising the bow and nocking takes before the string can be pulled at all (let go inside it and nothing flies -- owner, 2026-10-14), `drawTimeMs` how long the pull from brace to a full draw then takes, `drawMoveScale` / `drawSwayScale` the walk speed and the gait's side-to-side sway while drawn (owner 2026-10-14: 40% slower, 80% less sway), `minDraw` the least draw that looses an arrow at all (a tap is a fumble, not a shot), `ammo` the item id it shoots (consumed one per shot from the pack or hotbar; none = no shot). Speed = eased draw fraction x drawSpeedMps. 50 m/s is a real longbow's (was 65, a modern compound bow's, until 2026-10-13: owner, 'they move too fast'); the drop is real too, ~1 m over 20 m, which the NPC archers' holdover (ArrowHoldover) pays and the player aims over by eye. Art: scripts/gen_bow_items.py.
items.desc: A self longbow of yew as tall as a man's chin, braced with a waxed linen string. Hold to draw, let go to loose; the longer the draw, the harder it flies.

items.//: AMMUNITION (kind ammo): carried, never held or worn; a bow shoots it. `startCount` is how many the stub starting kit hands out (one stack, in the pack). The `arrow` block is the PENETRATOR it flies as (phys/kerf.h Penetrator): `massKg`, `tipRadius` in FINE cells (1/80 m), `sharpness` 0..1, and `damage` -- a FLAT hp charge on whatever it gets INTO (embedded or through; a glance pays only its trauma), on top of the tissue the channel destroys, the way a sword's `damage` is its cut. The head's HARDNESS is the material of the art's foremost cell (steel), unless `hardness` overrides it. Calibrated so 3-5 body arrows kill a man and the brain charge, not a rule, decides a head shot (the `arrow` gate prints both). EMBEDS, it does not go through (owner, 2026-10-13): `sharpness` 0.8 at the bow's 50 m/s (37.5 J, ~30 J of a perfect point's bite) stops a full draw ~9 cm into a torso, ~5 cm into an upper arm (it gets through the bone and stops in the far muscle) and inside the brain behind a side-on skull; only thin matter -- a hand, a scrap, a board -- leaves it speed to fly on with. It STAYS only when it went in at least its head's length (the art's head, 5 cm; game/arrows.h ArrowHeadIn, owner 2026-10-14): a shallower stop does its harm and drops out, so a 3/4 draw into a chest stays and a half draw falls out. The `pierce` gate prints every channel; the `arrow` gate's (h) every embed's head depth.
items.desc: A war arrow of spruce with a steel bodkin and goose fletching. It buries itself in whatever it strikes.

items.//: A QUIVER (kind quiver, docs/PLAN_poison_arrows.md, game/quiver.h). Worn on the BACK (equipment slot Back; Q or E on it in the hotbar puts it there), and the ONLY thing a bow draws from: no quiver on your back, no shot -- arrows loose in the pack are carried, not shot. It holds `quiver.capacity` of `quiver.ammo`, each arrow its OWN object (its own lattice, its own coat), so a poisoned arrow stays poisoned and a bloody one pulled out of a body stays bloody, while the quiver is still one slot. The bow draws a RANDOM arrow out of it each shot -- keep a poisoned quiver and a plain one and swap them on your back to choose. Drag arrows onto it to load it; picked-up and pulled arrows go into the worn one first. Coats on arrows in a quiver are FROZEN (the pack's rule). Open it on the item stage (double-click) to brush poison onto an arrow and copy that coat onto the rest. Drawn render-only on the rig's `back` socket, never carved (not damageable, for now). Art: scripts/gen_quiver_item.py.
items.desc: A stitched leather quiver with a turned wooden base, slung over the right shoulder. Your bow draws from the one on your back -- whichever arrow the hand finds first.

items.//: SHIELDS (kind shield, src/game/item.h ShieldSpec). Held in a hand slot like a weapon, but that hand's button RAISES it instead of swinging. WHAT IT STOPS IS ITS ART: a blade whose swept edge meets the shield's own voxels in their live pose is arrested (MobSystem::FindShieldBlock), raised or not -- so coverage is how big the shield is and where the arm holds it, and a shield hacked or burnt through has a hole a blade passes. The `shield` block is what HOLDING IT UP COSTS, in proportion to how far up it is: `raiseMs`/`lowerMs` to come up and go down; `moveScale` on the walk; `turnDegPerSec`, the most the body turns while raised (the shield faces where the body faces, so a fighter who circles you outpaces your guard); `stability`, the heaviest blow it holds against (impact = cut/2 x heft + blunt x (1 + armorBreak), times the blow's power: a full sword cut is ~9, a full mace blow ~29) -- above it the guard is beaten open and cannot come back up for `staggerMs`; `wear` x melee.blockItemDamage of each blow comes off its hp (sidecar `hp`; at 0 it breaks apart); `bluntThrough` of a blow's trauma reaches the arm behind it. And the other hand cannot start a swing while it is up (melee.shieldStrikeBelow). `clip` names the raise pose (assets/anims, authored for the right fist). Art and grips: scripts/gen_shield_items.py.
items.desc: Boards of wood under a hollow steel boss, bound at the rim in rawhide: a round shield as wide as your shoulders. Raised, it covers you from the hips to the eyes and slows everything else you do. Blades bite into it and fire takes it, and a mace will beat it aside.

A steel dish the width of a hand span, gripped in the fist behind a deep boss. It snaps up and costs you almost nothing to hold, and it covers almost nothing either: it stops the blade you put it in front of. A committed cut knocks it aside.

Boards faced with a sheet of iron and bound in steel, carried on a grip and a forearm strap. The face does not burn and a sword only scores it; it is also a slab of iron on one arm, and while it is up you walk like it.
